title: AI Assistants: The “Polyamorous” Approach
contentHtml:
Trend Overview:

  • Professionals are using multiple AI tools for specific tasks instead of relying on a single assistant.

  • Termed the “Polyamorous AI” approach, confirmed by industry analysis.

Versatile AI Tools

  • ChatGPT (OpenAI) – All-purpose AI: quick answers, life coaching, personal finance, general tasks.

  • Claude (Anthropic) – Writing support, document analysis, code generation, Slack reading for communication advice.

  • Grok (xAI / Twitter/X) – Real-time info, in-depth responses (legal, complex questions), fast interactions.

  • Gemini (Google) – Multimodal tasks, seamless Google ecosystem integration (Gmail, Docs, Sheets).

  • Perplexity AI – Research-focused, real-time, citation-backed answers.

  • GitHub Copilot (Microsoft/GitHub) – Developer-focused coding assistance and workflow support.

  • AlphaFold (Google DeepMind) – Protein structure prediction, e.g., used to cure a dog’s cancer.

  • Other mentions: DeepSeek, Meta AI – part of the wider AI ecosystem.

Business & Agency Platforms

  • Agencies are shifting to software-like service delivery using proprietary platforms.

  • WPP Open / Open Pro – Marketing and advertising AI platform.

  • Omni / Omni+ (Omnicom) – Data, audience, and content platform with strategic acquisitions.

  • The Machine (Stagwell) – AI for agency services, showcased at CES 2026.

  • Converged (Havas) – End-to-end data and content management.

  • Monks.Flow (Monks) – Digital-first marketing suite.

  • Cogito (Birlasoft) – Delivery optimization and AI-led solutioning.

  • AAVA (Ascendion) – Agentic engineering platform, AI adoption program.

  • AVA+ (Persistent) – GenAI platform for engineering and enterprise delivery.

Service-as-Software (SaS) & Enterprise Tools

  • SaS Concept: Generate value through platforms, reusable assets, and AI agents instead of linear headcount.

  • HFS Non-Linearity Index: Tracks decoupling of revenue from employee growth.

  • Claude for Excel (Anthropic): Pre-built skills for financial analysts, accountants, and wealth managers; integrates S&P Capital IQ, Moody’s, PitchBook.

  • Frontier Alliance (OpenAI + Accenture/BCG/Capgemini/McKinsey): Deploying AI agents into enterprise workflows.

Real-World AI Applications

  • Dog Cancer Cure: ChatGPT, AlphaFold, Grok + DNA sequencing labs → custom vaccine by an Australian entrepreneur.

  • Retail Expansion Tracker: Claude + Perplexity → live dashboard tracking retailer expansions/contractions via earnings calls & press releases.

  • Tax Evasion Detection: Generative AI + data software → Indian officials analyzed 60 TB of restaurant billing data.

  • Sludge Audit (Yomitan Village, Japan): AI tools improved medical check-up services by reducing administrative friction.

Key Takeaways

  • Multi-Tool Strategy: Choose AI assistants based on strengths: Claude for writing, Perplexity for research, Grok for real-time info.

  • Service-as-Software Shift: Agencies moving from headcount-based to platform-led delivery → margin growth from 30–40% → 55–65%.

  • Data as Moat: User-generated data becomes a critical asset for AI training (e.g., Niantic / Pokémon Go).

  • “Good Taste” Factor: Value shifts to human judgment, curation, and liability, areas AI cannot replicate.

title: Summary of the podcast conversation between Caroline, Paul Graham, and the host (referred to as “Carolyn” in the transcript), based on the provided text.
description: Summary of the podcast discussion involving Caroline, Paul Graham, and the host (referred to as “Carolyn” in the transcript), based on the provided text.
contentHtml:
Summary of the podcast discussion involving Caroline, Paul Graham, and the host (referred to as “Carolyn” in the transcript), based on the provided text.

Part 1: The Organic Growth of Y Combinator

  • Early Growth: Paul explains that YC grew organically without a deliberate marketing plan. Growth came from alumni telling their friends, Paul’s essays, and later, Hacker News.

  • The “Tiger Mom” Problem: The New York Times article (by Jenny Lee) was valuable not just for reaching founders, but for reaching parents. In the early days, parents worried that their kids were just “unemployed,” so a known brand like YC legitimized the path for families.

  • The Secret to Success: Paul believes the core reason for YC’s growth was that they genuinely helped startups. Alumni spread the word to their friends, creating a recipe for exponential growth within the tight-knit programmer community.

Part 2: The Challenges and Stress of Running YC

  • Hacker News as a Stressor: Paul admits that running Hacker News was a massive source of stress, responsible for more than half of his total stress from running YC. This included technical issues (server space, denial-of-service attacks) and community management (terrible fights on the site).

  • Negative Press and “Wokeness”: Paul and Caroline describe a period where YC faced intense scrutiny as a “consumer brand” in venture capital. This coincided with the rise of “wokeness” around 2012, leading to constant attacks and Twitter mobs based on lies.

    • The Peter Thiel Incident: A major controversy arose when a mob tried to force YC to “fire” Peter Thiel for being a Republican. Ironically, Sam Altman had been planning to remove him as a part-time partner simply because he was too busy to participate. YC refused to fire him, not wanting to set a precedent of yielding to a political mob.

  • The Reality of the Job: Most of Paul’s time was spent dealing with “knotty problems” for startups that ultimately failed, not the future giants like Airbnb. The stress from being attacked in the press often exceeded the stress of the actual work.

Part 3: The Hands-On Work with Startups

  • Office Hours and Advising: Paul was deeply involved in hands-on advising. He built all of YC’s original software and was known for helping founders with everything from naming their companies to refining their ideas.

  • Demo Day Preparation: Paul played a critical role in preparing founders for Demo Day. He focused on identifying the “vertebrae”—the five key sentences investors would remember. He would act like a playwright, drilling founders on their delivery, often telling them to talk slower.

  • Types of Office Hours:

    • Inflection Point: For promising but struggling startups, this was a session with multiple partners to try and “save” the company.

    • Palliative Care: For doomed startups with no hope, partners would switch to “palliative care mode”—being extremely kind and gentle to ensure the founders felt supported as their startup faded.

Part 4: The Sam Altman Era and Transition

  • Sam’s Early Days: Paul recognized Sam Altman instantly as a rare talent, comparing him to a 19-year-old Bill Gates. Sam was always around YC and was the obvious choice to succeed Paul.

  • The “Firing” Myth: Paul and Caroline debunk the myth that Sam was fired. Instead, Sam became distracted by other ambitious projects (like OpenAI and UBI research) after taking over.

  • The Transition to Gary Tan: When Sam chose to focus fully on OpenAI, they agreed to find a successor. Jeff was the first choice, but after he stepped down, Gary Tan became president. Paul notes that Gary has the energy, founder experience, and LP credibility that make him a great fit, leading to a period where there are finally no nagging worries about YC’s leadership.

Part 5: Paul’s Current Views and Q&A

  • Balance: Paul retired in part to spend more time with his family, though he notes YC was always well-suited for having kids.

  • Surprising Trends: He is shocked by the trend of founders (17-18 years old) skipping college and the massive increase in valuations (he cites a 60 million cap, which is 20 times Airbnb’s post-money valuation at Demo Day).

  • The Impact of AI:

    • AI hasn’t structurally changed startup advice yet, but it is a major source of new startup ideas.

    • Paul’s key defense against AI replacing founders is that the best ideas come from human needs (e.g., Airbnb came from needing rent money), and AIs have no needs.

  • Current Role: Paul remains energized by advising founders, not out of pure benevolence, but because he is genuinely interested in their ideas, which he compares to a constant stream of new puzzles.

title: What Do We Mean by “Universal”?
description: A three‑part framework for minds, machines, and the space of all possibilities
contentHtml:
A three‑part framework for minds, machines, and the space of all possibilities

We often talk about universality—universal computation, universal properties of language, universal intelligence—but the term gets used so loosely that it can obscure more than it clarifies. In a recent conversation, we dug into a more precise way to think about universality, one that turns out to be especially useful when we’re asking what an artificial general intelligence (or a human mind) actually needs to be capable of.

The core idea is simple: any claim about universality can be broken into three pieces—a system, a relationship, and a set.

System X has relationship R to every member of set S.

That’s it. The power comes from choosing those three variables carefully.

1. The Three Variables

  • System – What are we talking about? A computer, a brain, a language feature (like nouns), a strand of DNA.

  • Relationship – How does the system connect to the members of the set? “Contains,” “can simulate,” “can create,” “is essential for,” “can use” – all are possible relationships.

  • Set – What is the domain we care about? All human languages, all computable functions, all possible physical transformations, all explanations.

When someone says “nouns are a universal feature of human languages,” they are making a claim of this form:

  • System = nouns

  • Relationships are present in

  • Set = all human languages

The claim is about a finite set of existing languages. But when we talk about minds and AGI, the set we’re usually interested in is infinite: all possible programs, or all possible explanations, or all possible physical transformations that could be useful.

2. The Pivot: Some vs. All

The most fundamental distinction in universality is between some and all.

A system that can do some things—even many impressive things—is fundamentally different from a system that can do all things (in a given set). This is the difference between a machine that comes with a fixed set of built‑in programs and a universal Turing machine that can, given a recipe, execute any program.

Ironically, the universal Turing machine is the most boring in one sense: it has no special programs built in. It just waits for you to give it a description of what to do. That’s why universality is a qualitative boundary, not just a matter of scaling up performance. You can’t get to universality by adding more and more fixed capabilities; you have to flip to an architecture that can handle any capability when needed.

3. The Set That Matters: Everything Computable

For AGI, the natural set is all possible computable functions—or, more concretely, all programs. A system that can, in principle, produce any program (relativity, rocket designs, new mathematics) is universal in the “reachability” sense. But that’s not enough.

If all you can do is eventually grind out any program by brute‑force search, you’re technically universal, but practically useless. So we have to add two more requirements:

  1. Efficiency/tractability – You need to be able to find valuable programs in a reasonable amount of time. That means having the ability to compose existing ideas, to take large leaps in the space of programs, not just step one atom at a time.

  2. Use – It’s not enough to create an idea; you have to be able to use it. Use includes running it, combining it with other ideas, and—critically—using it as a criterion to judge other ideas.

This leads to a picture of intelligence as a system that can:

  • Reach any point in the space of possible programs (universality).

  • Navigate that space efficiently, using higher‑level abstractions (composition, reuse).

  • Recognize which points are valuable (criteria).

  • Exploit valuable points to reach further, faster (closing the loop).

4. The Architecture Question: Graphs, Not Hierarchies

How do you build a system with those properties? One hint comes from comparing knowledge representations.

A strict hierarchy (folders, outlines) is efficient for certain queries but rigid. A graph—where ideas are nodes and connections are links—is much more flexible. When you form a new idea by combining existing concepts, in a graph architecture the new node inherits all the connections of its parts almost for free. The result is that new knowledge is instantly integrated into the old web, ready to be used.

This is reminiscent of the “structural sharing” trick in programming languages (like Clojure’s persistent data structures): you can create a new version of something without copying the whole world. The brain seems to work that way, too: you can take the concept “table” (already richly connected) and “computer” and form “my computer is on the table,” and that new thought is immediately linked to everything you already know about tables and computers.

So the architecture matters not just for storage, but for the speed of recombination, which is the engine of efficient universality.

5. The Three Pillars

In the conversation, we noted that the approach we’re interested in rests on three pillars that set it apart from mainstream AI:

  1. Popperian problem‑solving – knowledge grows through conjecture and criticism, not just induction from data.

  2. Universality – focus on the qualitative boundary of being able to do anything, not just incremental performance improvements.

  3. Explanatory knowledge – treat explanations as a special kind of knowledge that compresses and generalizes in ways that mere patterns cannot.

When you put them together, you get a research direction that is less about tweaking benchmarks and more about understanding the architecture that makes open‑ended creation possible.

6. The Paradox of the Universal Machine

One final twist: the universal Turing machine is the most powerful in theory, yet it’s the least capable when you first turn it on. It has no built‑in knowledge. All its power is latent.

That’s the deep parallel with human minds. We aren’t born with relativity or calculus; we’re born with a process that can create them. The task for AGI is not to hard‑code more and more knowledge, but to build a system that can generate knowledge—and then use what it generates to generate more, in a virtuous cycle.

That’s the kind of universality worth aiming for.

This post is a summary of a longer discussion on the nature of universality, minds, and AGI. The conversation explored how a simple three‑part framework—system, relationship, set—can help clarify what we’re actually after when we say we want a universal intelligence.

title: Modern Loneliness
contentHtml:
Key Takeaways

  • Prioritize meaningful connections even if they require effort and vulnerability.

  • Feeling lonely is not just about being alone; it can happen even when surrounded by people.

  • Social media can increase feelings of loneliness by creating unrealistic comparisons.

  • The new cultural challenge is emotional connection. Many believe if they just had more friends or social activities, they’d feel less lonely.

  • I often tell myself: If I just join that group, or go to that event more often, I’ll finally feel connected. The problem is that by the time I get there, expectations have shifted, and I still feel disconnected.

  • At some point, I realized I had to redefine what connection means for me. I started to appreciate small, authentic moments rather than broad social approval.

  • Taking care of your mental health and emotional needs is crucial for overcoming loneliness.

Meet a Typical Modern Life
Working full-time with a busy schedule and multiple commitments, many people find themselves feeling lonely despite social calendars filled with acquaintances.

Questions that arise often are:

  • Am I truly connecting with others?

  • Am I doing enough to nurture my relationships?

  • Will I be okay emotionally?

The Numbers

  • A person in their 30s-40s, working full-time, managing family or personal responsibilities.

  • Active on social media and involved in community activities.

  • Has a few close friends but often feels a lack of deeper connection.

  • Prioritizes work and responsibilities over social life due to time constraints.

  • Seeks to build meaningful relationships and emotional security over time.

Social Media and Loneliness: What’s Going On?

People often think that being connected online is the same as being connected emotionally. It’s not.

Scrolling through curated images and status updates can make one feel even more isolated, because everyone else seems to have it all together.

What Can Help?

  • Focus on quality over quantity: deepen a few relationships rather than trying to maintain many superficial ones.

  • Seek professional help or therapy if feelings of loneliness persist.

  • Be mindful of social media usage and set healthy boundaries.

  • Engage in activities that promote genuine interaction, such as volunteering or joining small interest groups.

Are We Connected Enough?

There’s no perfect number of friends or events that solves loneliness. It’s about nurturing authenticity and vulnerability in relationships.

Loneliness is complex, and overcoming it often means changing how we relate to ourselves as much as how we relate to others.

Final Thought

Loneliness isn’t a sign of personal failure; it’s a modern challenge that many face. Understanding it, accepting it, and taking intentional steps toward emotional connection can lead to a more fulfilling and less lonely life.

title: When was the last time you felt completely invisible in a room full of people?
description: You put on a mask every day
contentHtml:
Not just physically alone, but swallowed by a crushing loneliness that no one sees or talks about. That ache that sits heavy in your chest, even when everyone around you is laughing and chatting. You put on a mask every day — a smile, a laugh, the “I’m fine” routine — but inside, you’re breaking. Anxiety gnaws at your thoughts, loneliness creeps into your bones, and yet you hide it because admitting it feels like weakness.

The world tells you to perform, to be strong, to keep your struggles private. Social media shows everyone else’s highlight reel, making you feel like the odd one out. But that curated perfection is a lie. Behind every filtered photo is someone fighting the same battles you are. Anxiety makes your mind race in circles, spinning worries into panic attacks. Loneliness feels like a void no one can fill. It’s exhausting. It’s isolating. And it’s more common than you think.

You might feel like screaming into the void, but the silence only makes the pain louder. That silence, that pretending, can push you deeper into despair. But here’s a truth no one tells you enough: it’s okay to not be okay. It’s okay to admit that the weight of anxiety and loneliness is crushing you. It’s the first step to breaking free.

Small steps matter. Say the words out loud — “I’m struggling.” Write it down if saying it feels impossible. Reach out to one person, anyone you trust, even if it’s terrifying. You don’t have to fix everything overnight. Just naming your feelings takes power away from them. Finding real connection isn’t about hundreds of followers or acquaintances; it’s about one genuine conversation, one shared moment of vulnerability.

When anxiety tightens its grip, ground yourself. Feel your feet on the floor, focus on your breath — slow, steady, real. Remind yourself that this feeling, as intense as it is, will pass. You’re not broken, just human. And human beings need connection. You’re not alone in this. There’s a whole quiet army of people who feel exactly how you do, even if they don’t say it out loud.

Break the silence. Share your story. Ask for help. Because the first step to healing is letting someone in. You don’t have to fight this alone anymore. Today, take one honest step toward breaking your silence. The pain is real. The loneliness is real. But so is your strength. You’re not invisible. You’re not alone. And there’s hope waiting on the other side of this darkness.

title: You’re Not ‘Just Tired’ — You’re Exhausted From Pretending)
contentHtml:
You’re not just tired. Stop telling yourself that lie.

You wake up every morning carrying the weight of a thousand silent screams — anxiety twisting your stomach, loneliness settling like a stone in your chest. But the world only sees a smile, a “I’m fine,” a nod that says “I’m handling it.”

The truth? You’re exhausted.

Not from work, or school, or the usual grind. You’re exhausted from pretending. From hiding how you really feel. From showing up like you have it all together when inside, you’re falling apart.

We live in a world that demands perfection and smiles — but rewards silence about the dark stuff. So you suffer alone, ashamed to admit you’re struggling.

This stops now.

Here’s the truth no one tells you: Your pain is valid. Your anxiety is not a weakness. Your loneliness is not your fault.

If you feel like no one hears you, if you’re drowning in your own mind — you’re not alone. And you don’t have to pretend anymore.

Starting today, let’s stop playing the role of “fine.” Let’s start naming the pain. Sharing the discomfort. Healing together, one honest word at a time.

Draft: Discussion Prompt (Title: When Was the Last Time You Felt Truly Alone?)

I want to hear from you — no filters, no masks.

When was the last time you felt truly alone?

Not just physically by yourself, but deeply, crushingly alone — like you were trapped inside your own mind, screaming for connection but hearing only silence.

What did that feel like? What did you do? How did you cope — or not?

Reply below. Your story matters.

This is a safe space to say the words you might never say out loud.
